On MRI, clear cell carcinoma is typically hyperintense on T2 and heterogeneous, with necrosis, hemorrhage or cysts. It enhances strongly and early in the arterial (corticomedullary) phase. It can lose signal on opposed-phase images because of intracellular lipid (microscopic fat), not to be confused with the macroscopic fat of angiomyolipoma, which loses signal on fat-suppressed sequences. Diffusion: variable restriction, not specific.
Comparison: papillary carcinoma is hypointense on T2, homogeneous, poorly vascularized and with slow enhancement; chromophobe has intermediate enhancement and may have a central scar; oncocytoma may show a central scar and enhancement inversion, but cannot be reliably distinguished from carcinoma.
Gadoxetate (20-minute hepatobiliary phase) is for the liver, not for the kidney.
